schema: biocast parameter file v1 (same shape as mechanics_params.json / micp_kinetics_params.json)

meta.track: elastomer / silicone mould path: transport across the mould face, hardness-to-modulus conversion, mould-rubber mechanicals, and 28-day alkaline compatibility
meta.purpose: numeric inputs for the silicone (and rigid-jacket) mould path of a parametric geometry generator for architectural objects cast from construction-waste aggregate bio-cemented by Bacillus subtilis MICP; companion to mechanics_params.json and micp_kinetics_params.json and follows the same schema

evidence_classes.MEASURED: value reported in a retrieved paper, standard, or named product datasheet; the quoted wording or table location is given in notes, and the source type is named explicitly (a manufacturer TDS is labelled as such, never passed off as peer review)
evidence_classes.DERIVED: computed by us from reported values; the arithmetic is shown in notes
evidence_classes.ASSUMED: engineering default with no source; the basis is stated in notes

retrieval_level_values.manufacturer_tds: supplier technical data sheet for a named product and grade — a legitimate source for a product property, NOT peer review
retrieval_level_values.manufacturer_literature: supplier technical bulletin stating a general relation rather than a product property
retrieval_level_values.our_arithmetic: computed here from rows in this or a companion file
retrieval_level_values.our_derivation: derived here from geometry or first principles
retrieval_level_values.reasoned_no_source: no source retrieved at the conditions of interest; the chain of reasoning is written out in notes so it can be attacked
retrieval_level_values.unsourced: widely repeated figure for which no primary source was retrieved; retained only as a cross-check, flagged not to be used in a model

meta.headline_finding: A silicone mould face is a NO-FLUX boundary for both oxygen and water vapour, which inverts the naive expectation. A 6 mm silicone skin carries ~294x the diffusive O2 resistance of the 26 mm DRAINED aggregate wall behind it, while against SATURATED pores the same skin adds under 1 % (ratio 0.0064). PDMS beats water and loses to air by two and a half orders of magnitude, and MICP needs drained pores. Water vapour: the skin passes 0.85 g/(m2 day) at cure conditions, 0.57 % of the 150 g/(m2 day) the drying model assumes for an open face, collapsing L_dry at 28 d from 21.0 mm to 0.12 mm. Silicone buys undercut tolerance and zero-draft release, NOT breathability. Only genuinely OPEN area is atmosphere.
meta.condition_mismatch_warning: The biocast case is 30 degC, 28 days, ~pH 9 (B. subtilis non-ureolytic route, initial culture pH 9 per micp_kinetics_params.json), in contact with a calcium/urea cementation solution. NOT ONE retrieved source measured a property at those conditions. The permeability data are at 40 degC on unfilled optical-grade RTV; the alkaline-aging data are at pH 13.5 and 40-70 degC on a 76 Shore A membrane; the mould-rubber mechanicals are supplier TDS values on virgin dry rubber after 7 days at 23 degC; the polyester hydrolysis data are at 0.1-2.8 M NaOH. Every row carries its own mismatch flag. Most mismatches are in the SEVERE direction (harsher than biocast), so conclusions drawn from them are conservative — but the mould-rubber mechanicals are the exception: they are virgin-material values and alkaline exposure moves them the wrong way.
two_most_load_bearing_numbers: O2 resistance ratio skin/drained-wall = 294x (220-505x across the 350-800 Barrer envelope) — see 'R_skin/R_wall,drained'; this is what makes a closed silicone mould a no-flux face
undercut strain eps = sqrt(1+(2u/s)^2) - 1, giving u/s_max ~ 0.75 at SF 4 — see 'eps(u/s)' and 'u/s_max'; this is why undercuts are NOT the binding limit for an elastomeric skin
weakest_rows: WVTR_tds — the 2000 g/(m2 day) at 50 um figure has NO retrieved primary source and no stated test condition; kept only as a cross-check, explicitly not for use in a model

Expected condition of a silicone mould skin after one 28-day biocast cure — reasoned from an Arrhenius extrapolation of pH 13.5 / 40-70 degC data down to pH 9 / 30 degC, with no measurement at the target conditions and no basis at all for cumulative damage over a mould library
E(SA)_exp — the base-e vs base-10 provenance ambiguity means the same published constants yield 2.159 or 5.884 MPa at Shore 60A, a 2.7x spread; usable only below ~40A
meta.single_measurement_that_would_most_impro: Shore A and Die B tear strength on the actual mould rubber after 28 d immersion in the actual cementation solution at 30 degC, repeated after 1, 5 and 10 simulated cure cycles. This is a durometer, a tear die and a beaker, and it would replace the weakest row in the file with a measurement at the real conditions.
meta.not_covered: This file does not size the rigid jacket (see mould.py mix_pressure / wall_deflection), does not address release agents or surface-cure inhibition, and carries no data on whether the cementation solution or the B. subtilis culture is affected by contact with silicone — that is a wet-lab question and out of scope.

parameters.name: O2 permeability of addition-cure silicone rubber (PDMS)
parameters.source_title: Vapour sorption and permeation properties of poly(dimethylsiloxane) films
parameters.notes: Blume et al. 1991, Table 1 ('Liquid permeability and sorption of organic solvents through silicone rubber'): oxygen 600 Barrer, nitrogen 280 Barrer, water 23,000 Barrer, measured on films of two-component RTV 615 (General Electric), crosslinked by addition hydrosilylation. TEST-CONDITION MISMATCH, FLAGGED: the table footnote states 'Temperature: 40 degC; 1 barrer = 1e-10 cm3(STP)-cm/(cm2-sec-cmHg)'. The biocast cure runs at 30 degC, so the as-reported 600 Barrer is ~10 K hot; gas permeability in PDMS rises with temperature, so 600 slightly OVERSTATES the 30 degC value and the no-flux conclusion drawn from it is conservative in the safe direction. GRADE MISMATCH: RTV 615 is an unfilled/lightly-filled optical-grade addition silicone, not a filled mould rubber; silica or carbonate filler LOWERS gas permeability, again in the conservative direction. The low/high bounds 350-800 are the commonly quoted spread for PDMS-family elastomers and are NOT from this table - treat the bounds as a convention and 600 as the single retrieved measurement. O2/N2 = 600/280 = 2.14, the canonical PDMS selectivity, which is the check that the film was defect-free rather than pinholed.

parameters.name: Barrer to SI permeability conversion factor
parameters.units: mol m / (m2 s Pa) per Barrer
parameters.source_title: Definition of the Barrer; SI unit algebra
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: 1 Barrer = 1e-10 cm3(STP)*cm/(cm2*s*cmHg). Convert each factor: cm3(STP) -> mol by dividing by the molar volume 22414 cm3/mol; cm -> m by 1e-2; per cm2 -> per m2 by 1e4; per cmHg -> per Pa by dividing by 1333.22 Pa/cmHg. So k = 1e-10 / 22414 * 1e-2 * 1e4 / 1333.22 = 3.3464e-16 mol*m/(m2*s*Pa). The project's working constant 3.348e-16 agrees to within 0.05 % (ratio 0.9995) - the small difference is whether 22414 or 22400 cm3/mol is used for the STP molar volume. Either is fine; do not chase the fourth digit.

parameters.name: O2 permeability of silicone rubber, SI units
parameters.source_title: Vapour sorption and permeation properties of poly(dimethylsiloxane) films
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: 600 Barrer * 3.3464e-16 = 2.009e-13 mol*m/(m2*s*Pa). Bounds from 350 and 800 Barrer: 1.172e-13 and 2.678e-13. This is the number that enters the resistance comparison against the pore body; the 40 degC / unfilled-grade mismatches carried by the parent row apply unchanged.

parameters.name: Gas-phase O2 permeability of a DRAINED MICP pore body
parameters.substrate: packed crushed-waste aggregate, phi = 0.40, air-filled pores
parameters.source_title: Computed from micp_kinetics_params.json D_O2_gas_eff and the ideal gas law
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: for gas-filled pores the concentration that pairs with a partial-pressure driving force is C = p/(RT), so the permeability is P = D_eff/(RT). With D_O2_gas_eff = 6.46e-7 m2/s (micp_kinetics_params.json, Millington-Quirk at phi = 0.40, drained), R = 8.3145 J/(mol K) and T = 303.15 K: P = 6.46e-7/(8.3145*303.15) = 2.563e-10 mol*m/(m2*s*Pa). CONSISTENCY NOTE: an earlier working value of 2.32e-10 appears in this project's session notes; the 10 % difference is the choice of D_eff within its own 3.05e-8 to 1.98e-6 range, not an error in either. Nothing downstream turns on it - the skin-to-wall ratio is a factor of ~300 either way.

parameters.name: Dissolved-phase O2 permeability of a SATURATED MICP pore body
parameters.substrate: packed crushed-waste aggregate, phi = 0.40, water-filled pores
parameters.source_title: Computed from micp_kinetics_params.json D_O2_eff_sat and Henry solubility of O2 in water
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: P = D_eff * S where S is the Henry solubility on a partial-pressure basis. Dissolved O2 in water at 30 degC in equilibrium with air is 0.234 mol/m3 at p_O2 = 0.2095*101325 = 21228 Pa, so S = 0.234/21228 = 1.102e-5 mol/(m3 Pa). With D_O2_eff_sat = 5.05e-10 m2/s (micp_kinetics_params.json): P = 5.567e-15 mol*m/(m2*s*Pa). DRAINED/SATURATED RATIO = 2.563e-10 / 5.567e-15 = 46,000x. This is the single mechanistic fact the whole silicone argument rests on: drainage, not the mould material, is what delivers oxygen.

parameters.name: Assumed silicone skin thickness for an architectural-scale mould
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE. Basis: 6 mm is a plausible brush-on or poured skin for a mould of the size cast in this project (object spans 190-400 mm), thick enough to survive repeated demoulding and thin enough not to consume unreasonable volumes of rubber. Bounds 3-12 mm bracket the range of skin thicknesses used in practice for architectural mouldmaking. EVERY transport row below that quotes a thickness uses this 6 mm value, so if the skin is redesigned all of those numbers scale: O2 resistance scales linearly with thickness, WVTR inversely.

parameters.name: Diffusive O2 resistance ratio: 6 mm silicone skin vs 26 mm DRAINED pore wall
parameters.substrate: 6 mm silicone skin over 26 mm drained aggregate wall
parameters.source_title: Computed from P_O2,sil,SI and P_pore,gas at the two thicknesses
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: series diffusive resistance of a slab is R = L/P. Skin: R = 0.006/2.009e-13 = 2.99e10. Drained 26 mm wall (the measured vessel wall, ShellParams(wall = 26.0)): R = 0.026/2.563e-10 = 1.01e8. Ratio = 294. Bounds come from carrying the 350-800 Barrer envelope: 800 Barrer gives 220x, 350 Barrer gives 505x. THIS IS THE HEADLINE FINDING AND IT INVERTS THE NAIVE EXPECTATION. PDMS is famously O2-permeable, so a silicone mould 'should' breathe; it does not, because the thing it is being compared against is air in drained pores, and air beats PDMS by two and a half orders of magnitude. A silicone mould face is a NO-FLUX boundary for oxygen.

parameters.name: Diffusive O2 resistance ratio: 6 mm silicone skin vs 26 mm SATURATED pore wall
parameters.substrate: 6 mm silicone skin over 26 mm saturated aggregate wall
parameters.source_title: Computed from P_O2,sil,SI and P_pore,sat at the two thicknesses
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: R_wall,sat = 0.026/5.567e-15 = 4.67e12, against R_skin = 2.99e10, so ratio = 0.0064. WHY THE INTUITION MISLEADS: against water-filled pores the silicone skin is essentially transparent - it adds under 1 % to the resistance. PDMS genuinely beats water by a wide margin, and that true fact is what makes 'silicone breathes' feel right. It loses to AIR. Both rows are needed to state the finding honestly: silicone is a good oxygen conductor compared with the wrong reference and a poor one compared with the right one. An earlier working value of 0.0009 in this project's session notes used a lower saturated-pore diffusivity; the conclusion (skin negligible against saturated pores) is identical.

parameters.name: Water vapour permeability of addition-cure silicone rubber
parameters.source_title: Vapour sorption and permeation properties of poly(dimethylsiloxane) films
parameters.notes: Blume et al. 1991, Table 1, SAME FILM AND SAME TABLE as the 600 Barrer oxygen value - which is why this pair can be compared without an inter-study correction. Water 23,000 Barrer at 40 degC, i.e. 38x the oxygen permeability, with reported sorption 0.38 g/100 g. Silicone is the most vapour-permeable common elastomer and this row is the quantitative form of that reputation. TEST-CONDITION MISMATCH: 40 degC, against a 30 degC cure. Bounds 15,000-30,000 are a convention bracketing grade-to-grade variation, not measurements from this table.

parameters.name: WVTR of a 6 mm silicone skin at the BIOCAST CURE CONDITION (30 degC, saturated inside to 90 % RH outside)
parameters.source_title: Vapour sorption and permeation properties of poly(dimethylsiloxane) films
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC, and the thickness is stated because WVTR without a thickness is meaningless. Flux = P * dp / L, converted to mass: P_H2O = 23000 * 3.3464e-16 = 7.697e-12 mol*m/(m2*s*Pa). Driving force: saturation vapour pressure of water at 30 degC is 4246 Pa (steam table); inside the mould the pore air is saturated (a = 1.0), outside it is the cure-chamber 90 % RH (micp_kinetics_params.json RH_cure = 95 %, range 90-100 %), so dp = 0.10 * 4246 = 425 Pa. Flux = 7.697e-12 * 425 / 0.006 = 5.45e-7 mol/(m2 s); * 18.015 g/mol * 86400 s/day = 0.848 g/(m2 day). Bounds carry the 15,000-30,000 Barrer envelope. NOTE the driving force is the binding term, not the permeability: at 95 % RH the flux halves again, and at 100 % RH it is zero.

parameters.name: WVTR of a 6 mm silicone skin at a full-gradient ASTM-style test condition (38 degC, 100 % -> 0 % RH)
parameters.source_title: Vapour sorption and permeation properties of poly(dimethylsiloxane) films
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC, computed only as a cross-check against manufacturer WVTR figures, which are quoted at full gradient and at 38 degC (100 degF), not at cure conditions. dp = p_sat(38 degC) = 6632 Pa; flux = 7.697e-12 * 6632 / 0.006 * 18.015 * 86400 = 13.25 g/(m2 day). THIS IS 15.6x THE CURE-CONDITION VALUE, entirely because of the driving force - which is the reason a supplier WVTR number cannot be dropped into a cure model unconverted. The cross-check succeeds: scaling a commonly quoted 2000 g/(m2 day) at 50 um film by inverse thickness to 6 mm gives 16.7 g/(m2 day), agreeing with this independent Blume-based route to 21 %.

parameters.name: Commonly quoted WVTR of thin silicone film, and its inverse-thickness scaling to 6 mm
parameters.units: g / (m2 day) at 6 mm, from 2000 g/(m2 day) at 50 um
parameters.substrate: thin silicone film, unstated test condition
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE FOR THE 2000 g/(m2 day) AT 50 um FIGURE. It is widely repeated for thin silicone membrane and appears in this project's session notes, but no datasheet, paper or standard behind it was retrieved, and no test temperature or RH gradient travels with it - which is exactly the defect this file is meant to prevent. Retained ONLY as an order-of-magnitude cross-check on WVTR_test, which it matches to 21 %. Scaling arithmetic: 2000 * (50e-6 / 0.006) = 16.7 g/(m2 day), valid only if transport is Fickian and thickness-limited, which for PDMS above a few hundred nm it is. DO NOT USE THIS ROW IN A MODEL - use WVTR_cure.

parameters.name: Free-evaporation vapour flux the drying model assumes, at the same 90 % RH driving force
parameters.substrate: open (unmoulded) drained aggregate face at 90 % RH
parameters.source_title: Computed from micp_kinetics_params.json E_crit and RH_cure
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: E_crit = 1.5 mm/day (range 0.5-2.5) is the stage-1 evaporation rate the drying model uses; the effective flux at RH is E_crit*(1-RH). At RH = 0.90: 1.5 * 0.10 = 0.15 mm/day of liquid water, and 1 mm/day over 1 m2 is 1000 g/day, so J_free = 150 g/(m2 day). The comparison that matters: the 6 mm silicone skin passes 0.848 g/(m2 day), which is 0.57 % of this. A silicone face is a no-flux boundary for water vapour too.

parameters.name: Drying penetration depth BEHIND a 6 mm silicone face at 28 d, and the section ceiling it implies
parameters.substrate: 26 mm aggregate wall behind a 6 mm silicone skin, 28 d, 30 degC, 90 % RH
parameters.source_title: Computed from the project drying relation with the silicone-limited flux substituted for free evaporation
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: the project drying relation is L_dry = E(1-RH)t/(phi*dS), and the section ceiling is 2*L_dry (drying from both faces). Open face, 28 d, 90 % RH, phi = 0.40, dS = 0.5: L_dry = 1.5*0.10*28/(0.40*0.5) = 21.0 mm, ceiling 42.0 mm - this reproduces the project's established open-face numbers exactly, which is the check that the substitution below is done consistently. Behind the skin the effective E is the silicone-limited flux 0.848 g/(m2 day) = 8.48e-4 mm/day of water, already inclusive of the RH driving force: L_dry = 8.48e-4*28/(0.40*0.5) = 0.119 mm, ceiling 0.237 mm. INTERPRETATION: a fully silicone-enclosed body does not drain, so gas-phase oxygen transport never switches on and the cemented fraction stays at the saturated-pore value. Only genuinely OPEN area is atmosphere. Silicone buys undercut tolerance and zero-draft release, NOT breathability. An earlier working value of 0.23 mm for L_dry appears in this project's session notes; it used the 16.7 g/(m2 day) full-gradient figure rather than the cure-condition flux, so it is ~2x optimistic. Both are far below any castable section, so the design conclusion is unchanged.

parameters.name: Shore A to Young's modulus, ASTM-style exponential form
parameters.units: MPa (value is a function of Shore A; low/high are SA = 15 and SA = 60)
parameters.source_title: Dow Corning technical bulletin 11-3716-01 'Durometer Hardness for Silicones' (Larson, 'Can You Estimate Modulus From Durometer Hardness for Silicones?')
parameters.notes: RELATION: E [MPa] = exp(0.0235*SA - 0.6403). CLASSIFIED MEASURED ONLY IN THE WEAK SENSE THAT THE RELATION IS PUBLISHED, NOT THAT WE RETRIEVED ITS UNDERLYING DATASET - the named source is a Dow technical bulletin (product literature, not peer review) and no DOI exists; it is reproduced in the same form by many secondary sources. PROVENANCE AMBIGUITY WORTH KNOWING: the Dow bulletin and several other primary statements of this relation write it as log10(E) = 0.0235*S - 0.6403, i.e. BASE 10, whereas the widely propagated engineering form uses exp(), i.e. base e. These are NOT the same function - at SA = 30 they give 1.161 and 1.067 MPa (close, 8 % apart), but at SA = 60 they give 5.884 and 2.159 MPa (2.7x apart). The base-e form is the one used in this project and the one tabulated in the low/high bounds here (SA 15 -> 0.750, SA 60 -> 2.159 MPa). USE ONLY BELOW ~40A, where the two conventions and Gent all agree to within 25 %. The same bulletin states plainly that all such correlations were 'created empirically and suffer from a common issue - significant scatter'. The nominally valid range is SA 20 to 80.

parameters.name: Shore A to Young's modulus, Gent 1958 relation
parameters.units: MPa (value is a function of Shore A; low/high are SA = 15 and SA = 60)
parameters.source_title: On the Relation between Indentation Hardness and Young's Modulus
parameters.notes: RELATION: E [MPa] = 0.0981*(56 + 7.62336*SA) / (0.137505*(254 - 2.54*SA)). Gent 1958 derives the hardness-modulus relation 'from classical elasticity theory' rather than empirically, and the abstract states the theoretical relation is 'more appropriate than the empirical one for small indentations' and that 'the numerical constants are not subject to experimental uncertainty' - which is the reason to prefer it where the two disagree. The paper's own caveat is that the relation is validated for hardness above about 40 B.S. & I.R.H. and that reduced major loads are needed below 35-40 for it to apply across the range - so at Shore 15-30, the softness range of interest for mould rubbers, THIS RELATION IS BEING USED BELOW ITS VALIDATED WINDOW. Full text was not retrievable (closed access); the relation and its caveats are taken from the abstract plus the form as tabulated in secondary engineering sources. Tabulated here: SA 15 -> 0.563, SA 30 -> 1.142, SA 50 -> 2.456, SA 60 -> 3.605 MPa.

parameters.name: Divergence between the two Shore-A-to-modulus relations
parameters.source_title: Both relations evaluated at matched Shore A
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC, both formulae evaluated at the same hardness: SA 15 -> 0.563/0.750 = 0.75; SA 20 -> 0.87; SA 30 -> 1.142/1.067 = 1.07; SA 40 -> 1.25; SA 50 -> 2.456/1.707 = 1.44; SA 60 -> 1.67. SO THE CHOICE OF RELATION DOES NOT MATTER AT SHORE 30A (7 % apart, well inside the scatter either relation admits) AND DOES MATTER ABOVE ABOUT 40A (25 % at 40A, 44 % at 50A, 67 % at 60A). Practical rule for this project: mould skins are specified at 15A-30A, so quote ~1.1 MPa at Shore 30A and do not agonise over which relation produced it; if a harder jacket-side rubber above 40A is ever specified, state which relation was used and treat the modulus as a factor-of-1.5 quantity. A third data point, Qi, Joyce & Boyce 2003 (10.5254/1.3547752), maps durometer to a neo-Hookean modulus by finite-element simulation of the indentation itself and concludes the durometer test 'still can be used as a reasonable approximation of the initial neo-Hookean modulus unless the limiting extensibility is known to be small' - i.e. the mapping degrades exactly for materials that cannot stretch far, which mould silicones can.

parameters.name: Young's modulus of a Shore 30A mould silicone
parameters.source_title: Consensus of the exponential, base-10 and Gent relations at SA = 30
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC at SA = 30: exp form 1.067 MPa; base-10 form 1.161 MPa; Gent 1.142 MPa. All three within 8 %, so the interval is a genuine tie and 1.10 MPa is quoted as the midpoint. CROSS-CHECK AGAINST DIRECT TENSILE MEASUREMENT, WITH A GRADE MISMATCH: Johnston et al. 2014 (10.1088/0960-1317/24/3/035017) measured bulk Sylgard 184 across curing temperatures 25-200 degC and report Young's modulus 1.32-2.97 MPa at hardness 44-54 ShA. Reading their pair together, ~1.3 MPa at 44 ShA is BELOW all three hardness correlations at that hardness (1.35 exp, 1.99 base-10, 1.93 Gent), which is a useful reminder that these correlations carry real scatter against direct tension. Sylgard 184 is an electronics-grade encapsulant, not a mould rubber.

parameters.name: Tensile strength, tin-cure (condensation) mould silicone, Shore 30A
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max 30 technical bulletin (ASTM D-412)
parameters.notes: SUPPLIER TECHNICAL DATA SHEET, NOT PEER REVIEW - labelled accordingly. Product and grade: Smooth-On Mold Max 30, a tin-cure (condensation) mould silicone, Shore 30A, mixed 100A:10B by weight. TDS values, all measured after 7 days at 23 degC: tensile strength 3.98 MPa, 100 % modulus 758 kPa, elongation at break 300 %, Die B tear strength 21.9 kN/m (ASTM D-624), specific gravity 1.18 g/cc, shrinkage 0.002 in/in = 2.0 mm/m, useful temperature range -54 to 204 degC. TEST-CONDITION MISMATCH: 23 degC, 7-day cure, dry, virgin rubber - NOT 30 degC under 28 days of contact with an alkaline calcium/urea solution. No supplier reports properties after that exposure. Low bound 2.75 MPa is the Mold Max XLS II figure (550 psi, same series, extra-low-shrinkage tin grade) as a within-family spread.

parameters.name: Tensile strength, platinum-cure (addition) mould silicone, Shore 30A
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Star 30 technical bulletin (ASTM D-412)
parameters.notes: SUPPLIER TECHNICAL DATA SHEET, NOT PEER REVIEW - labelled accordingly. Product and grade: Smooth-On Mold Star 30, a platinum-cure (addition) mould silicone, Shore 30A, mixed 1A:1B by volume. TDS values, all measured after 7 days at 23 degC: tensile strength 420 psi = 2.90 MPa, 100 % modulus 96 psi = 0.662 MPa, elongation at break 339 %, Die B tear strength 88 pli = 15.4 kN/m, specific gravity 1.12 g/cc, shrinkage < 0.001 in/in = < 1.0 mm/m, useful temperature range -53 to 232 degC. Same 23 degC / dry / virgin mismatch against the biocast cure applies. Bounds from the sibling grades in the same TDS table: Mold Star 15/16 at 400 psi = 2.76 MPa and Mold Star 31T at 423 psi = 2.92 MPa. NOTE THE COMPARISON WITH THE TIN GRADE: at equal Shore 30A the tin-cure rubber is the STRONGER in tension (3.98 vs 2.90 MPa, +37 %) and the TOUGHER in tear (21.9 vs 15.4 kN/m, +42 %). Tin-cure is not the weaker chemistry mechanically; its disadvantages are shrinkage and library life, below.

parameters.name: Elongation at break, tin-cure vs platinum-cure mould silicone, Shore 30A
parameters.substrate: Mold Max 30 (tin) and Mold Star series (platinum)
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max 30 and Mold Star 15/16/30/31T technical bulletins (ASTM D-412)
parameters.notes: Tin-cure Mold Max 30: 300 %. Platinum-cure Mold Star 30: 339 %; the softer Mold Star 15/16 at Shore 15-16A reach 440 %, and the translucent Mold Star 19T/20T reach 740 % at Shore 19-20A. So elongation buys back what hardness costs, and a softer grade is the lever if a deep undercut needs more stretch. Range 300-440 % spans the two Shore-30A chemistries plus the soft platinum grades. For context outside the mould-rubber class, Smooth-On Ecoflex 30 (a very soft platinum silicone, Shore 00-30) is tabulated at 900 % elongation in the peer-reviewed literature (10.3390/polym12051031, Table 1, reproduced from the supplier SDS) - a demonstration that the 250-300 % figure often assumed for 'silicone' is a mould-grade property, not a silicone property. SUPPLIER TDS, 23 degC, 7-day cure, dry virgin rubber; no post-alkaline-exposure data exists.

parameters.name: Die B tear strength, tin-cure vs platinum-cure mould silicone, Shore 30A
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max 30 and Mold Star 30 technical bulletins (ASTM D-624)
parameters.notes: Tin-cure Mold Max 30: 21.9 kN/m (= 125 pli). Platinum-cure Mold Star 30: 88 pli = 15.4 kN/m. Mold Max XLS II: 110 pli = 19.3 kN/m. Mold Star 19T/20T/31T: 90 pli = 15.8 kN/m. TEAR, NOT TENSILE, IS THE PROPERTY THAT KILLS MOULDS: a mould fails at a nick propagating from a thin web or a sharp internal corner during demoulding, which is the same notch-sensitivity argument this project applies to the cast object itself. Design implication: fillet the SILICONE's internal corners as well as the object's. SUPPLIER TDS, ASTM D-624 Die B, 23 degC, dry.

parameters.name: Density of filled mould silicone
parameters.substrate: filled mould silicone, tin and platinum grades
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max and Mold Star series technical bulletins (ASTM D-1475, specific gravity)
parameters.notes: SUPPLIER TDS. Mold Max 30 (tin) 1.18; Mold Max XLS II 1.22; Mold Star 30 (platinum) 1.12; Mold Star 15/16 1.18; Mold Star 19T/20T/31T 1.08; Ecoflex 30/50 1.07. Value 1.15 is the midpoint of the mould-grade cluster. MASS-PER-MOULD ARITHMETIC (DERIVED from this row): a 6 mm skin is rho * 0.006 m = 6.7 to 7.3 kg per square metre of mould face at 1.12 to 1.22 g/cc. For the vessel and block moulds in this project that is the number that decides whether the silicone or the rigid jacket dominates the cost.

parameters.name: Linear cure shrinkage, tin-cure vs platinum-cure mould silicone
parameters.substrate: Mold Max (tin) and Mold Star (platinum) series
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max 30 and Mold Star series technical bulletins (ASTM D-2566)
parameters.notes: SUPPLIER TDS. Tin-cure Mold Max 30: 0.002 in/in = 2.0 mm/m = 0.2 %. Platinum-cure Mold Star series: < 0.001 in/in = < 1.0 mm/m = < 0.1 %. Ecoflex: < 0.001 in/in. Condensation cure evolves a small molecule (typically an alcohol) and shrinks; addition cure does not and does not. WHY THIS MATTERS HERE: on a 400 mm object 0.2 % is 0.8 mm of dimensional error, which is comparable to the 2-3 mm Panot relief tolerance and to the measured 2.49 mm/face block relief, so a tin-cure skin is dimensionally significant at architectural scale. Platinum cure is the correct choice on dimensional grounds. The same TDS series also notes that accelerating a tin-cure silicone 'will result in a shorter library life of the mold' - tin-cure rubbers revert over time; platinum-cure ones do not.

parameters.name: Service temperature range of mould silicone
parameters.substrate: Mold Max (tin) and Mold Star (platinum) series
parameters.source_title: Smooth-On Mold Max and Mold Star series technical bulletins
parameters.notes: SUPPLIER TDS. Tin-cure Mold Max series: -19 to 205 degC (one bulletin) / -54 to 204 degC (another) - the supplier's own literature is internally inconsistent at the cold end, which is a reason to treat the bound as indicative. Platinum-cure Mold Star series: -53 to 232 degC. NOT A BINDING CONSTRAINT FOR THIS PROJECT: the biocast cure runs at 30 degC (micp_kinetics T_cure = 30, range 25-37), two orders of magnitude inside the envelope. Recorded because a hot-water or steam sterilisation step, if ever added, would still be inside it.

parameters.name: Activation energy for alkaline (nucleophilic) hydrolysis of the siloxane backbone
parameters.source_title: Degradation and service-life prediction of silicone rubber in a highly alkaline environment simulating concrete
parameters.notes: Masson et al. 2022 (Engineering Failure Analysis; NRC Canada) reports, citing Lewis: 'an activation energy (Ea) of 96 kJ/mol for the water driven degradation (hydrolysis) of straight chain polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a process of random attack of water onto Si-O-Si bonds', and then that 'In acidic or alkaline water, where an electrophile or nucleophile can polarize Si-O-Si segments, the hydrolysis reaction readily proceeds because of a lower activation energy of 21 kJ/mol'. THE SILOXANE BACKBONE IS NOT INERT TO BASE - alkali catalyses its scission and drops the barrier by a factor of 4.6. Value = 21 (the alkaline case, the relevant one); high bound 96 = the neutral-water case, recorded so the contrast is legible.

parameters.name: Measured alkaline aging behaviour of a silicone membrane, pH 13.5, 40-70 degC, up to 30 days
parameters.substrate: commercial silicone membrane ('Silicone X'), carbonate-filled, initial 76 Shore A
parameters.source_title: Degradation and service-life prediction of silicone rubber in a highly alkaline environment simulating concrete
parameters.notes: THE MOST CONDITION-RELEVANT RETRIEVED MEASUREMENT, AND ALSO THE MOST OVER-SEVERE - both must be stated. Method: 'A silicone membrane was immersed in a pH 13.5 solution and aged up to 30 days at four temperatures between 40degC and 70degC', per ASTM D7705, pH 13.5 chosen as 'representative of the pH at the surface of fresh concrete'. Findings: the rubber STIFFENS rather than softening - Shore A rose from an initial 76 upward over time, rubbery-plateau storage modulus E' rose past the paper's own 4 MPa failure criterion (about 10 days at 60 degC, more than 40 days at 40 degC), relative crosslink density roughly tripled by 30 days at 70 degC, and FTIR showed 'a loss of methyl content' from the Si-CH3 peaks at 1260 and 798 cm-1. Cracking was photographed at 23 d/50 degC and 14 d/60-70 degC. Dakin-Arrhenius on the stiffening kinetics gave Ea = 60 kJ/mol and a predicted service life 'just over 1 year'. MISMATCH FLAGS, ALL IN THE SEVERE DIRECTION: (i) pH 13.5 is roughly 4.5 pH units above the biocast non-ureolytic cure, which micp_kinetics records at initial culture pH 9 (B. subtilis growth optimum 7-9), so the hydroxide activity driving scission is ~30,000x lower here; (ii) the lowest test temperature was 40 degC against a 30 degC cure; (iii) the specimen was a thin free film of a 76 Shore A product, not a 6 mm 30A mould skin. The paper itself cautions that its 1-year prediction is 'a very short time in comparison with established performance for silicones in construction' where 'Sealants, for instance, will readily perform well over 20 years'. USE THIS ROW AS THE MECHANISM AND THE FAILURE MODE (stiffening, embrittlement, surface cracking - NOT dissolution), NOT AS A LIFETIME FOR THIS APPLICATION.

parameters.name: Expected condition of a silicone mould skin after one 28-day biocast cure
parameters.substrate: Shore 30A mould silicone, 28 d, 30 degC, pH ~9 calcium/urea cementation solution
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE AT THE ACTUAL CONDITIONS. Reasoning, stated so it can be attacked: the only retrieved alkaline-aging dataset (Masson et al. 2022, above) ran at pH 13.5 and 40-70 degC and needed 10-40 days to reach its stiffening failure criterion. The biocast cure is 28 days at 30 degC and roughly pH 9. Scaling the Masson et al. Ea = 60 kJ/mol from 40 degC to 30 degC alone slows the stiffening by exp[(60000/8.314)*(1/303.15 - 1/313.15)] = 2.1x, and the four-and-a-half-decade lower hydroxide activity is a far larger factor again on a nucleophile-catalysed reaction. ONE cure should therefore leave a 30A mould skin serviceable. WHAT IS NOT SUPPORTED: any claim about cumulative damage over a mould library of 10 or 50 cures, because the exposure is repeated and the Masson et al. failure mode (crosslinking, hardening, surface crack initiation) is cumulative and irreversible. THE SINGLE MEASUREMENT THAT WOULD MOST IMPROVE THIS FILE: Shore A and Die B tear on the actual mould rubber after 28 d immersion in the actual cementation solution at 30 degC, repeated for 1, 5 and 10 cycles. That is a durometer, a tear die and a beaker.

parameters.name: Hydrolytic stability of PLA under warm wet alkaline conditions
parameters.source_title: Surface Etching of 3D Printed Poly(lactic acid) with NaOH: A Systematic Approach
parameters.notes: THE PROJECT RECORD'S CLAIM THAT PLA HYDROLYSES UNDER WARM WET ALKALINE CONDITIONS IS SUPPORTABLE IN MECHANISM BUT THE RETRIEVED DATA DO NOT SUPPORT IT AT BIOCAST CONDITIONS - and the honest answer is that the mismatch is large. Schneider et al. 2020 treated 3D-printed PLA scaffolds in 0.1-5.0 mol/L NaOH for 1 min to 48 h and report: 'For NaOH concentrations up to 0.2 mol/L, no height changes are observed even at extended periods of time'; 'After 48 h and NaOH concentrations of 3.0 mol/L and higher, the PLA scaffolds dissolve completely'; erosion rate rises linearly with NaOH up to 3.0 mol/L. Crucially, for bulk properties: 'the treatment has no effect on the E-modulus of the scaffolds' (4.5 +/- 1.6 GPa before and after) and strain at break was likewise unchanged - the attack is a SURFACE erosion at these times. MISMATCH: 0.2 mol/L NaOH is pH ~13.3 and even that produced no dimensional change; the biocast cure is pH ~9, i.e. ~20,000x less hydroxide, at 30 degC rather than the study's room temperature, but for 28 days rather than 48 h. The retrieved evidence therefore does NOT establish that a PLA mould fails in one biocast cure. What it does establish is the mechanism and its concentration dependence. Laycock et al. 2017 (10.1016/j.progpolymsci.2017.02.004) supplies the mechanistic frame: ester hydrolysis 'can be either acid or base catalysed', the uncatalysed rate 'is low when in air or water at neutral pH', PLA degrades by BULK not surface erosion so molecular weight falls before any mass loss appears, and the tabulated half-life of a polyester bond in neutral water at 25 degC is 3.3 years. A 28-day exposure at pH 9 and 30 degC will not dissolve a PLA mould; it may plausibly reduce molecular weight and embrittle it, and that damage is invisible on inspection and cumulative across a mould library. RECOMMENDATION: do not use PLA for a reusable mould, on the strength of the mechanism plus invisibility of the damage, and say that this is a mechanism-based judgement rather than a measurement at these conditions.

parameters.name: Hydrolytic stability of PET/PETG under warm wet alkaline conditions
parameters.source_title: Alkaline Hydrolysis Kinetics of Poly(ethylene terephthalate) Fibers
parameters.notes: THE PROJECT RECORD'S CLAIM THAT 'PETG HOLDS' IS ONLY PARTLY SUPPORTABLE, AND THE HONEST STATEMENT IS THAT PETG IS ALSO A POLYESTER AND ALSO BASE-HYDROLYSABLE - it is slower, not immune. Kawahara et al. 2016 etched PET fibres in 1.0-2.8 M NaOH at 40-60 degC and found activation energies 'concentrated within the range of 62.4-69.5 kJ/mol', reporting a previous value of 64.9 kJ/mol, and that hydrolysis proceeds as a TOPOCHEMICAL (surface) attack with a rectilinear diameter-versus-time relation - the fibre thins from outside in rather than degrading through the bulk. That surface-limited mode is the real reason PET/PETG outperforms PLA for a mould: damage stays at the surface where it is visible and does not embrittle the section. TWO MISMATCHES: (i) the study is PET homopolymer FIBRE, oriented and semicrystalline, whereas PETG is the glycol-modified amorphous copolymer used for 3D printing - amorphous regions hydrolyse faster, so PETG should be somewhat LESS resistant than these fibres, and no PETG-specific alkaline dataset was retrieved; (ii) 1.0-2.8 M NaOH at 40-60 degC is far above pH ~9 at 30 degC. VERDICT AS SUPPORTED: PETG > PLA for a reusable biocast mould, on the mechanism (surface vs bulk erosion) rather than on any measurement at biocast conditions. Both are polyesters; neither is silicone.

parameters.name: Ranking of candidate mould materials for 28-day alkaline cure contact
parameters.substrate: silicone vs PETG vs PLA, 28 d, 30 degC, pH ~9 cementation solution
parameters.notes: NO SINGLE RETRIEVED SOURCE COMPARES THESE THREE AT BIOCAST CONDITIONS; this row is an ordinal judgement built from the three sourced rows above and is labelled ASSUMED for that reason. RANKING, best first: (1) SILICONE - the Si-O backbone is base-catalysed-hydrolysable (Ea 21 kJ/mol alkaline vs 96 neutral) but the measured failure mode at pH 13.5 is STIFFENING over 10-40 days, and biocast runs 4.5 pH units milder and 10 K cooler; (2) PETG - polyester, base-hydrolysable, but the retrieved kinetics are TOPOCHEMICAL/surface, so damage is visible and does not embrittle the section; (3) PLA - polyester, base-hydrolysable, and per Laycock the erosion mode is BULK, so molecular weight and toughness fall before any visible change. The ordering is driven by erosion MODE (surface vs bulk vs stiffening) more than by rate, because a mould is reused and invisible cumulative damage is the failure that matters. Rigid-jacket materials (plywood, GRP, 3D-printed PETG) sit outside this ranking when they never contact the wet mix.

parameters.name: Undercut strain relation for an elastomeric skin
parameters.units: dimensionless strain (low/high are u/s = 0.10 and u/s = 1.0)
parameters.substrate: elastomeric mould skin over a re-entrant feature
parameters.source_title: Geometric derivation; no source required
parameters.notes: DERIVATION, shown in full because the relation is the load-bearing one for the whole silicone path. Model the skin spanning an undercut as a straight chord of length s that must deform into the shallowest path clearing a re-entrant feature of depth u. Idealise that path as two straight legs from the chord ends to the deepest point: each leg has horizontal run s/2 and vertical rise u, so its length is sqrt((s/2)^2 + u^2), and the total stretched length is L = 2*sqrt((s/2)^2 + u^2) = s*sqrt(1 + (2u/s)^2). Engineering strain is then eps = L/s - 1 = sqrt(1 + (2u/s)^2) - 1, a function of the aspect ratio u/s alone with no absolute length scale - which is why a small deep undercut and a large deep one demand the same strain. Tabulated: u/s = 0.10 -> 2.0 %; 0.25 -> 11.8 %; 0.50 -> 41.4 %; 0.75 -> 80.3 %; 1.00 -> 123.6 %. TWO ASSUMPTIONS THAT MAKE THIS A LOWER BOUND ON THE TRUE STRAIN: strain is taken as uniform along the chord (real skins localise it at the undercut lip, so peak local strain is higher), and the two-straight-leg path is the shortest clearing path (a real skin bends around a radius, which is longer). Treat the result as optimistic by a factor that a 4x safety factor is meant to absorb.

parameters.name: Demould safety factor on elongation at break
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE. Basis, stated so it can be argued with: elongation at break is a single-pull property of virgin rubber measured on a dumbbell at a controlled rate (ASTM D-412), whereas a mould skin is stretched repeatedly, over a possibly nicked and abraded surface, at whatever rate a person pulls, after alkaline exposure that the Masson et al. data show causes stiffening (falling elongation). Four separate degradations of the tabulated property, hence 4x rather than the 2x that a single monotonic pull might justify; range 3-5 reflects that the choice is judgement, not measurement. CONSEQUENCE - AND THIS IS THE FINDING: at SF 4 on a Mold Star 30 platinum skin (EAB 339 %) the allowable strain is 84.8 %, which by eps(u/s) permits u/s up to 0.78. For Mold Max 30 tin (EAB 300 %) the allowable is 75.0 %, permitting u/s up to 0.72. For a soft Ecoflex-class rubber (EAB 900 %) the allowable is 225 %, permitting u/s up to 1.55. UNDERCUTS ARE NOT THE BINDING LIMIT FOR AN ELASTOMERIC SKIN: even u/s = 0.5, a deep undercut by any rigid-mould standard, needs only 41.4 % strain, half the allowable. The binding limits remain the ones this project already knows - aggregate bridging on the floor, drying on the ceiling - and now the no-flux boundary condition the skin itself imposes.

parameters.name: Maximum admissible undercut aspect ratio for an elastomeric skin at SF 4
parameters.source_title: Inversion of eps(u/s) at allowable strain = EAB/SF_demould
parameters.notes: ARITHMETIC: invert eps = sqrt(1+(2u/s)^2) - 1 to get u/s = 0.5*sqrt((1+eps)^2 - 1), evaluated at eps_allow = EAB/4. Mold Max 30 tin, EAB 300 %: eps_allow = 75.0 % -> u/s_max = 0.72. Mold Star 30 platinum, EAB 339 %: eps_allow = 84.8 % -> u/s_max = 0.78. Ecoflex 30, EAB 900 %: eps_allow = 225 % -> u/s_max = 1.55. Value 0.75 is the Shore-30A mould-grade figure (tin and platinum are a tie at this precision); low 0.72 and high 1.55 span tin-cure to soft-grade. INHERITS every caveat of its two parents: the strain relation is a lower bound (uniform-strain and shortest-path idealisations), the safety factor is judgement, and the EAB values are supplier TDS numbers on virgin dry rubber at 23 degC.

parameters.name: Rigid backing jacket ('mother mould') requirement
parameters.substrate: silicone skin plus rigid backing jacket
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE; this is standard mouldmaking practice recorded as a design rule with its mechanical rationale, because the parameter file is where the reader will look for it. The two functions are distinct and must not be conflated: THE SILICONE SKIN is what tolerates undercuts and permits zero-draft release (u/s_max = 0.75, above); THE RIGID JACKET is what holds the skin to shape against mix pressure. Order of magnitude for the second: at E_30A = 1.10 MPa the skin is roughly four orders of magnitude less stiff than a plywood or GRP jacket, so an unbacked skin does not resist the hydrostatic and granular pressure of the wet mix - it bulges, and the cast section thickens uncontrollably, which matters because section thickness is the quantity the drying ceiling constrains. DISASSEMBLY ORDER IS JACKET-OFF-SKIN FIRST, THEN PEEL SKIN OFF THE CAST. Peeling with the jacket still on forces the skin to stretch against a rigid constraint and is how skins tear at their thin sections. This project's mix_pressure and wall_deflection helpers in mould.py size the jacket; they are not re-derived here.
